learningObjectives: Explain the benefits of modular reuse in application development.
Describe the five guiding principles of modular enterprise reuse.
Describe how the Situational Layer Cake and prescriptive design support modular reuse.
Identify how Dev Studio and App Studio enable reuse through studio interoperability.
Describe how the Reuse Library facilitates asset management.

elements.description: A software development approach that uses standardized, reusable components to build applications. Instead of starting from scratch, developers ASSEMBLE pre-built, tested modules to speed up development and maintain consistency across the enterprise.

Design: reduces planning time with ready-made components. Development: speeds builds and minimizes coding. Testing: limits defects/scope via pre-tested modules. Deployment: simplifies implementation with standardized components. Maintenance: enables automatic updates across all applications using shared modules.

elements.text: Reuse is like building with shipping containers instead of pouring concrete every time: standardized, pre-tested units snap together fast, and fixing one container design improves every building that uses it.

bulletPoints: Reuse benefits EVERY phase: Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance.
Assembling pre-tested modules is faster and more consistent than building from scratch.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: The Five Guiding Principles of Reuse

elements.description: Use consistent building blocks across applications AND authoring environments (App Studio and Dev Studio).
Individual components can be updated independently without disrupting the entire application or requiring changes to every consuming module.
Behavior can be adjusted through configuration settings without rewriting the underlying business logic, enabling business-led customization.
Applications are assembled from encapsulated, self-contained components rather than built as large monolithic layers that are difficult to maintain or update.
Establish governance (for example, a Pega Center of Excellence) to manage, evolve, and ensure the quality of reusable assets.

elements.text: Memory hook 'I-U-C-M-G': Interoperable, Updateable, Configurable, Modular, Governed — a reuse program needs all five, and Governance is the glue that keeps the other four trustworthy.

bulletPoints: A successful reuse program follows all five principles; the most-missed on exams are Configurable (no logic rewrite) and Governed (Center of Excellence).

elements.description: A patented Pega architecture that balances two competing forces: REUSE (economies of scale and consistency) and VARIATION (different products, regions, regulatory needs). It avoids both 'spaghetti' single-app if-then-else and the sprawl of 50–100 near-identical apps.
Core Pega Platform features and enterprise-wide reusable assets (e.g., a company-wide authentication module used across all applications).
Reusable components specific to a division (e.g., a claims-processing flow tailored for the insurance division but reused across its applications).
Application-specific implementations that leverage lower-layer assets (e.g., a customer-service app that uses shared authentication and claims components but adds its own workflows).
Customizations for specific deployment scenarios WITHOUT altering the base application (e.g., localizing the customer-service app for a region by adjusting language and regulatory rules).

elements.text: At runtime the layer cake looks across all layers and dynamically assembles the MOST SPECIFIC pieces — like ordering 'a UK loan onboarding' and the kitchen automatically plates the enterprise base, the lending variation, and the UK-specific topping, with no if-then-else code.

bulletPoints: Layers go most-general (Enterprise) to most-specific (Implementation); change higher layers without affecting lower ones, and preserve the base's integrity.
Real example: AIG consolidated 52 claim systems into one ('One Claim') using this architecture.

Reusable features are encapsulated in MODULE applications, which stack to form BUILT-ON applications (e.g., a reusable Meeting module / smart shape configured once in App Studio and reused across apps).

elements.description: A simplified, collaborative, inclusive authoring experience that lets a wide range of low-code practitioners understand, interpret, and author processes/applications. It hides complexity and raises Case Type literacy so stakeholders express requirements and feedback better.
Robust low-code environment for experienced architects to configure integrations, complex decisions, security, and advanced features beyond App Studio's scope.

elements.text: Dev Studio is the parts factory; App Studio is the assembly line. Architects fabricate and label reusable parts (relevant records) in the factory, and citizen developers snap them together on the line.

bulletPoints: Using Dev Studio together with App Studio maximizes Pega's power so everyone collaborates effectively in App Studio.
In Dev Studio: build advanced apps/components (traditional UI authoring, automated unit testing) and reusable modules; mark Rules as relevant records.
In App Studio: configure an application without code using AI-assisted development, the prescriptive UI, relevant records, and Configuration Sets.

elements.description: Rules marked as relevant records become available for assembly in App Studio, enabling Studio interoperability and exposing reusable assets to business-level authors.
When you create Fields, Views, Processes, and user actions in App Studio, Pega automatically marks them as relevant records.

elements.text: Marking a rule as a relevant record is like putting a tool on the pegboard outline: now anyone in App Studio can see it, grab it, and reuse it instead of digging through the whole toolbox.

bulletPoints: Rule types you can mark as relevant records include: Properties (fields), Paragraphs, Correspondences, Service-Level Agreements, Strategies, Processes (Flows), User actions (Flow Actions), Data Transforms, Decision Tables, Notifications, Pulse Feed Rules, Validate Rules, and When Rules.
Relevant records let you build powerful processes/automations/actions in Dev Studio and assemble them in App Studio.

elements.description: A centralized repository in App Studio that contains all reusable assets in the enterprise, helping developers of all skill levels discover, understand, and use reusable components. Combined with strong governance, it accelerates development, improves quality, and boosts agility.

elements.text: The Reuse Library is the enterprise's app-store-plus-card-catalog: a single, governed place to search, understand, and check out reusable assets — so teams stop reinventing the same component.

bulletPoints: To maximize value, establish processes/tools for: Lifecycle management (roles/processes; centralized or federated model), a Reuse catalog (tagging/search in a central governed catalog), Deployment and maintenance tracking (where assets are deployed), Value measurement (dashboards/reports on usage and ROI), and Education and advocacy (training, recognition, communicating benefits).
A successful reuse program depends on a clear governance framework providing leadership, coordination, and prioritization.

examPitfalls.title: Naming the five guiding principles
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Distractors invent principles or drop one. The set is Interoperable, Updateable, Configurable, Modular, Governed.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use 'I-U-C-M-G'; remember Configurable = adjust behavior without rewriting logic, and Governed = a Center of Excellence.

examPitfalls.title: Situational Layer Cake layer order/purpose
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The four layers (Enterprise, Division, Application, Implementation) and their purposes get swapped.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Enterprise = org-wide reuse; Division = division-specific reuse; Application = the app itself; Implementation = deployment/region customization without changing the base.

examPitfalls.title: What the layer cake balances
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates miss that it balances REUSE vs. VARIATION and avoids both spaghetti single-apps and app sprawl.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Tie it to the value: economies of scale/consistency (reuse) AND business/regional/regulatory variation — assembled most-specific at runtime, no if-then-else.

examPitfalls.title: Relevant records are the key to App Studio reuse
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Tests confuse where reusable modules are built vs. assembled. Build in Dev Studio; mark as relevant records; assemble in App Studio.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Dev Studio creates/marks; App Studio assembles. Fields, Views, Processes, and user actions created in App Studio are auto-marked as relevant records.

examPitfalls.title: Reuse Library lives in App Studio
examPitfalls.trapDescription: It is a centralized repository of reusable assets in App Studio, not a Dev Studio-only artifact.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Reuse Library = App Studio's central, governed catalog of reusable assets for all skill levels.

examPitfalls.title: Module applications vs. built-on applications
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Reusable features are encapsulated in module applications that STACK to form built-on applications.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Encapsulate reusable features in a module application (e.g., a Meeting smart shape) and stack it under built-on applications.

examPitfalls.title: Governance is required, not optional
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A reuse program without governance fails; the curriculum stresses a clear governance framework and Center of Excellence.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Pair the Reuse Library with governance: lifecycle management, catalog, deployment tracking, ROI measurement, education/advocacy.

examPitfalls.title: Reuse benefits span the whole lifecycle
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions limit reuse benefits to 'development.' They apply to Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Maintenance.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Recall all five phases; Maintenance benefit = automatic updates propagate across all apps using the shared module.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which THREE of the following are among the five guiding principles of modular enterprise reuse?
practiceQuiz.hint: The five are I-U-C-M-G; one option is the OPPOSITE of a principle.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The five principles are Interoperable, Updateable, Configurable, Modular, and Governed. 'Monolithic' is the opposite of the 'Modular' principle (which says avoid monolithic layers). No partial credit.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A bank needs a company-wide authentication module that every application across the enterprise can reuse. In the Situational Layer Cake, which layer should hold it?
practiceQuiz.hint: Enterprise-wide reusable assets belong at the layer shared across the entire organization.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Enterprise Layer holds core platform features and organization-wide reusable assets such as company-wide authentication. The Division layer is division-specific, Application is app-specific, and Implementation handles deployment or regional customization.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A team must localize a customer-service app for the UK — adjusting language and regulatory rules — WITHOUT altering the base application. Which layer is appropriate?
practiceQuiz.hint: This layer adds deployment-specific customization while leaving the base application intact.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Implementation Layer holds customizations for specific deployment scenarios — such as regional localization — without modifying the base application. Other layers serve organizational or application-level reuse, not deployment-specific variation.

practiceQuiz.scenario: At run time, how does the Situational Layer Cake decide what to execute for 'a UK loan onboarding'?

options.text: It looks across all layers and dynamically assembles the most-specific applicable pieces, no if-then-else code needed
It runs a giant if-then-else block embedded in one application
It deploys a separate app per variation and routes to it

practiceQuiz.hint: The Situational Layer Cake dynamically assembles the most-specific pieces across all layers.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Situational Layer Cake dynamically assembles the most-specific version of each rule across layers at run time, avoiding both complex if-then-else logic and the need to maintain a separate application per variation.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An architect builds a powerful Process and complex Decision Table in Dev Studio and wants citizen developers to be able to assemble them in the App Studio Case Designer. What must the architect do?

options.text: Mark the Rules as relevant records
Move the Rules into the Implementation Layer

practiceQuiz.hint: The 'key to marking rules reusable in App Studio.'
practiceQuiz.rationale: Relevant records make Dev Studio-built rules available for assembly in App Studio. Layer placement, deletion, and Access Roles do not expose rules to the Case Designer.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A System Architect is reviewing which Rule types can be surfaced as reusable assets in App Studio via relevant records. Which THREE Rule types can be marked as relevant records?
practiceQuiz.hint: Three are in the relevant-records list; one is a security/access construct.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Properties, Decision Tables, and SLAs are among the rule types that can be marked as relevant records (along with Paragraphs, Correspondences, Strategies, Processes, user actions, Data Transforms, Notifications, Pulse Feed Rules, Validate Rules, When Rules). Access Groups are not in that list. No partial credit.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which assets does Pega AUTOMATICALLY mark as relevant records when they are created in App Studio?

options.text: Fields, Views, Processes, and user actions

practiceQuiz.hint: The four things you most commonly build in App Studio.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Fields, Views, Processes, and user actions created in App Studio are automatically marked as relevant records, making them available for assembly. Other rule types — such as Data Transforms or SLAs — are not auto-marked and must be marked manually.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA wants to find a centralized repository of reusable assets without switching to Dev Studio. Where does the Reuse Library reside, and what is its purpose?

options.text: In App Studio — a centralized repository of all reusable assets for developers of all skill levels
In Admin Studio — for monitoring system resources
In Prediction Studio — for storing ML models
In the database — accessible only via SQL

practiceQuiz.hint: Think of a centralized, governed catalog where all skill levels can discover and reuse assets.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Reuse Library is App Studio's centralized repository of reusable assets, helping architects and business users at all skill levels discover, understand, and incorporate approved components without rebuilding them.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An enterprise wants to measure the return on investment of its reusable assets by asset and by consuming application. Which Reuse-Library practice covers this?

options.text: Value measurement — dashboards and reports on usage and ROI

practiceQuiz.hint: This function monitors dashboards and measures return on investment per reusable asset.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Value measurement uses dashboards and reports to monitor asset usage and ROI by asset and consuming application. The other functions handle roles and processes, catalog and search, and training respectively.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which Pega real-world example best illustrates the Situational Layer Cake consolidating siloed systems?

options.text: AIG consolidating 52 claim systems into one ('One Claim')
A team writing one giant if-then-else application
Deploying 100 separate apps that each do the same thing
Storing all data in a single spreadsheet

practiceQuiz.hint: Apply the CTO example from the curriculum: factory builds, assembly line assembles components.
practiceQuiz.rationale: AIG used the layer cake to consolidate 52 global claim systems into 'One Claim.' The other options are exactly the anti-patterns the layer cake avoids.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO statements correctly describe the roles of App Studio and Dev Studio in reuse?

options.text: Dev Studio is used to create reusable modules and mark Rules as relevant records
App Studio assembles reusable components without touching code, using the prescriptive UI and Configuration Sets
App Studio is where integrations and complex security are configured
Dev Studio cannot be used together with App Studio

practiceQuiz.hint: Dev Studio is the factory; App Studio is the assembly line using pre-built parts.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Dev Studio creates reusable modules and marks relevant records; App Studio assembles them code-free. Integrations/complex security are Dev Studio tasks (not App Studio), and the two studios are explicitly meant to work together. No partial credit.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which guiding principle means you can adjust a component's behavior WITHOUT rewriting business logic?
practiceQuiz.hint: Configurable means adjusting behavior through settings without rewriting the core logic.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Configurable = adjust behavior without rewriting business logic. Updateable = update components without disrupting apps; Interoperable = consistent blocks across apps/studios; Governed = manage/evolve/quality-assure assets.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A reusable Meeting-setup capability is needed by several business processes. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Create a reusable smart shape / module application, configure it once in App Studio, and reuse it across applications
Copy the meeting logic into each Case Type separately
Hard-code the meeting steps in every flow
Build a separate application per process

practiceQuiz.hint: Modular means encapsulating a component once so it can be reused many times.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Encapsulate the capability in a reusable smart shape/module application configured once and reused across apps — eliminating duplication and simplifying maintenance. The other options reintroduce duplication.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which Reuse-Library governance practice specifically tracks WHERE reusable assets are deployed across the organization?
practiceQuiz.hint: Tracking deployment and usage tells you where assets are used across consuming applications.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Deployment and maintenance tracks where reusable Pega assets are deployed and how they are consumed. The catalog function organizes and enables search, education builds a reuse culture, and value measurement reports ROI. These are distinct lifecycle functions.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is explaining the benefits of Pega's layered architecture to a client who is concerned about maintainability. Which statement correctly describes how the layered structure supports reuse?

options.text: You can change higher layers without affecting lower ones, preserving the base's integrity
Changing a lower layer automatically rewrites all higher layers
Each layer must duplicate the layer below it
Only the Implementation Layer can be reused

practiceQuiz.hint: Customize in the appropriate (higher) layer; protect the base.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The layered structure lets you modify higher layers without affecting lower ones, preserving the base and ensuring core updates apply across dependent apps. The other options contradict the model.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO lifecycle phases benefit from modular enterprise reuse, per the module?

options.text: Testing — fewer defects and reduced testing scope via pre-tested modules
Maintenance — automatic updates across all apps using shared modules

practiceQuiz.hint: Consider which lifecycle phases benefit most from reusing pre-tested, shared modules.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Testing benefits from reuse because pre-tested modules limit defect scope, and Maintenance benefits because updating a shared module propagates the fix everywhere it is used. Recruiting and procurement are not documented reuse lifecycle benefits. No partial credit.

quickRecap.value: Assemble standardized, pre-tested components instead of building from scratch.
Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance — maintenance updates propagate to all apps using a shared module.
Interoperable, Updateable, Configurable (no logic rewrite), Modular (avoid monoliths), Governed (Center of Excellence).
Balances reuse vs. variation. Layers: Enterprise → Division → Application → Implementation; runtime assembles most-specific pieces.
AIG: 52 claim systems → one 'One Claim.' Reusable features = module apps stacked into built-on apps.
Dev Studio creates reusable modules + marks relevant records; App Studio assembles code-free (prescriptive UI, Configuration Sets, AI-assist).
Key to App Studio reuse; mark rules in Dev Studio for assembly. App Studio auto-marks Fields, Views, Processes, user actions.
App Studio's central, governed catalog of reusable assets; governance = lifecycle mgmt, catalog, deployment tracking, ROI measurement, education.
